analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above roughly $200 million at annual rates up to 8 percent.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced; the committee has taken no further action and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds a new annual federal tax on wealth itself, not just income. A household would pay nothing until its net wealth passed roughly $200 million — 1,000 times the median household's wealth, with $50 million as a floor. Above that, rates start at 2 percent and climb to 8 percent on the largest fortunes, and trusts pay a flat 8 percent on everything above the threshold. The Treasury would have to audit at least 30 percent of covered taxpayers each year, and families whose wealth is tied up in a business could defer payment up to five years. The bill does not say what the revenue would fund.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the federal Treasury would collect a new stream of revenue paid only by households and trusts worth more than roughly $200 million. Ordinary taxpayers would benefit indirectly, if Congress later used that revenue for tax cuts, public programs, or deficit reduction — the bill itself attaches no spending to the money.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only to net wealth above a threshold set at 1,000 times the greater of $50,000 or the median household wealth, so nearly all households would owe nothing.

Rates are graduated on wealth above the threshold: 2 percent on the first tier, 4 percent on the next, 6 percent on the next, and 8 percent on the largest fortunes; trusts pay 8 percent above the threshold.
Tangible personal property worth $50,000 or less, such as ordinary household goods and cars, is excluded, and retirement trusts under section 401(a) and tax-exempt entities are exempt.
The bill requires the Treasury to audit at least 30 percent of taxpayers who owe the tax each year, and imposes penalties of 30 to 50 percent for large undervaluations of assets.

The tax reaches wealth held through grantor and beneficiary trusts, applies to assets a person would pass at death, and applies to covered expatriates as if the year ended before expatriation, closing common exits.

analysis.who_pays: A few thousand of the wealthiest households and large trusts, which would owe an annual tax of 2 to 8 percent on net wealth above the threshold.

drawbacks.text: Many assets of the richest households — private companies, art, real estate — have no market price. The bill requires Treasury to invent new valuation methods for assets that are not publicly traded, and applies penalties up to 50 percent for substantial valuation understatements, an acknowledgment that valuation disputes will be constant.

Families whose wealth is tied up in an operating business would owe tax each year on paper value they do not receive as income. The bill allows deferral for up to five years for severe liquidity constraints or hardship on an ongoing enterprise, but the tax could still eventually force asset sales.

The bill dedicates no revenue to any program. Its benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on a future Congress deciding what to do with the money; if the revenue were used for deficit reduction or unrelated priorities, most households would see no direct gain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is aimed narrowly — only fortunes above roughly $200 million pay — and it includes real carve-outs for small property, retirement accounts, and illiquid businesses, which answers the most common objections to earlier wealth-tax proposals. The serious practical cost is administration: valuing private companies and other unpriced assets every year would be contentious and litigated. And the bill stops short of saying what the money is for, so its public benefit is a promise about future decisions, not a guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Summer Lee of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on April 14, 2025.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Twelve Democrats had joined as cosponsors, and no further action appears in the bill's record.
The bill's text sets the threshold at 1,000 times the greater of $50,000 or median household wealth, with graduated rates of 2 to 8 percent above the threshold.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households and trusts above the threshold avoid a new annual tax of up to 8 percent for as long as the bill sits untouched in committee, and no new revenue reaches the Treasury.

for.name: Summer Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the wealth-tax bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee's only recorded action is the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors are House Democrats; the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee has not acted on the bill.

industries.note: Households with net worth above roughly $200 million would owe 2 to 8 percent of wealth above the threshold each year, with trust-held assets attributed to them. The tax never takes effect while the bill sits in committee.

Large trusts would pay a flat 8 percent above the threshold, and the bill's attribution rules treat trust assets as held by grantors and beneficiaries, undercutting trust structures used to shield wealth from annual taxation.

The bill authorizes Treasury to impose reporting duties on financial institutions and to require business entities to estimate their own value, adding compliance costs for companies owned by covered households.

analysis.trajectory: With a minority-party sponsor, no hearing or markup announced, and the Ways and Means Committee under Republican control, the bill is very unlikely to reach the House floor this Congress; wealth-tax proposals at this stage typically expire when the Congress ends.
